clinicalPearls: One of the more common single-gene causes of autism spectrum disorder combined with intellectual disability
Features include global developmental delay, autistic behaviour, hypotonia and frequent feeding problems in infancy
Early or premature eruption of the primary teeth is a distinctive and useful clue
Recurrent infections, visual problems, sleep disturbance and behavioural difficulties are common
Facial features are often described as a prominent forehead, a broad nasal bridge and a thin upper lip
Caused by heterozygous loss-of-function variants in ADNP, usually de novo and autosomal dominant, encoding a chromatin-associated transcription regulator essential for brain development
The strong association with autism means it should be considered in syndromic autism with intellectual disability
reference.pathophysiology: ADNP encodes the activity-dependent neuroprotector homeobox protein, a transcription factor that binds chromatin and, as part of the ChAHP complex with the chromatin remodeller CHD4 and HP1, regulates the expression of genes governing neuronal development, synapse formation and neuroprotection. Heterozygous loss-of-function variants, usually de novo, cause haploinsufficiency (and in some cases altered protein function), dysregulating these developmental gene programmes. The resulting disruption of cortical development and synaptic function produces autism, intellectual disability and the associated systemic features. Its role in chromatin-linked transcriptional control places it among the chromatin-related neurodevelopmental disorders.
additionalInvestigations: Dental review noting premature primary dentition
Brain MRI and EEG where clinically indicated
Chromosomal microarray and gene panel or exome sequencing including ADNP
redFlags: Feeding failure and faltering growth in infancy
Severe behavioural or sleep disturbance affecting the child and family
reference.prognosis: ADNP syndrome causes lifelong intellectual disability and autism of variable severity, with most individuals needing substantial support. Outcome depends on cognitive and behavioural severity, and care is supportive and multidisciplinary.
pitfalls: Labelling as idiopathic autism and not pursuing genetic testing in syndromic presentations
Overlooking premature dentition as a diagnostic clue
Attributing recurrent infections to unrelated causes
Assuming a normal MRI excludes a monogenic cause
management: Provide early developmental intervention with speech and language, occupational and physiotherapy and individualised special-education support
Address autistic features and behavioural difficulties with structured behavioural interventions
Manage infantile feeding problems and hypotonia with feeding support and nutritional monitoring
Arrange ophthalmological review, dental review for premature dentition, and management of sleep disturbance
Monitor for and treat recurrent infections, and investigate seizures with EEG where clinically indicated
Coordinate lifelong care through a multidisciplinary neurodevelopmental team
Offer genetic counselling regarding the usually de novo autosomal dominant cause and recurrence risk
